input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-632: Mobile Robot Programming. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course covers standard and novel techniques for mobile robot programming, including software architectures, reactive motion control, map building, localization and path planning. Other topics may include multiple robot systems, robot vision and non-traditional and dynamic robots. Students will implement various algorithms in simulation as well as on a real robot, and investigate and report on current research in the area. Course offered every other year. Prerequisites: CSCI-630 or CSCI-331 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring Regeneration revision 2: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[opencv-documentation]
Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays. Color conversion changes the coordinate representation of pixel values. Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure. Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns. Calibration estimates camera parameters needed for geometric measurement. Geometric transforms map coordinates between image representations. Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories. Motion methods compare observations across time. Results depend on sampling, illumination, noise, thresholds, coordinate frames, and evaluation metrics.

This course covers standard and novel techniques for mobile robot programming, including software architectures, reactive motion control, map building, localization and path planning. Other topics may include multiple robot systems, robot vision and non-traditional and dynamic robots. Students will implement various algorithms in simulation as well as on a real robot, and investigate and report on current research in the area. Course offered every other year. Prerequisites: CSCI-630 or CSCI-331 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

[ros-2-concepts]
ROS 2 organizes a robot application as nodes that communicate through typed interfaces. Topics support publish-subscribe streams, services support request-response interactions, and actions support longer-running goals with feedback and cancellation. Parameters configure node behavior. Coordinate transforms describe relationships among reference frames. Sensors produce observations that must be timestamped and interpreted in the correct frame. Robot software separates sensing, state estimation, planning, control, and actuation while making message contracts and timing assumptions explicit. Testing should consider latency, dropped messages, sensor noise, actuator limits, safety boundaries, and the difference between simulation and physical operation.

beats.claim: Robot software separates sensing, state estimation, planning, control, and actuation while making message contracts and timing assumptions explicit.
beats.example: A navigation stack uses a perception node to publish camera data, a localization node to estimate pose, a planner to generate waypoints, a controller to compute velocities, and an actuator driver to send commands to wheels.
beats.title: Robot Software Architecture Overview
beats.visualDirection: Display a layered block diagram showing five stacked modules (sensing, state estimation, planning, control, actuation) with bidirectional arrows indicating data flow and explicit timing labels on each interface.

beats.claim: ROS 2 organizes a robot application as nodes that communicate through typed interfaces, where topics support publish-subscribe streams, services support request-response, and actsa
beats.example: A localization node subscribes to a topic publishing IMU data, while a planning service handles a request-response call to compute a path between two waypoints.
beats.title: ROS 2 Node Communication Model
beats.visualDirection: Show a network diagram with labeled nodes connected by color-coded lines representing topics (dashed), services (solid), and actions (dotted), with message type tags on each line.

beats.claim: Parameters configure node behavior, allowing runtime adjustment of thresholds, gains, and operational limits without recompiling code.
beats.example: A controller node uses a parameter named 'max_speed' to cap wheel velocity, which can be updated via a ROS 2 parameter server during simulation.
beats.title: Parameter Configuration and Behavior
beats.visualDirection: Render a configuration panel with key-value pairs for robot parameters, highlighting how changing a single value propagates to the corresponding node's behavior settings.

beats.claim: Coordinate transforms describe relationships among reference frames, enabling accurate mapping of sensor data to the robot's global coordinate system.
beats.example: A camera's local image coordinates are transformed into the robot's base link frame using a rotation matrix and translation vector to align with the map.
beats.title: Coordinate Transforms and Reference Frames
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate two overlapping coordinate grids (local and global) with labeled axes, showing a transformation arrow and matrix notation connecting them.

beats.claim: Sensors produce observations that must be timestamped and interpreted in the correct frame to maintain synchronization across the system.
beats.example: LiDAR scans are tagged with a precise timestamp and attached to the robot's odometry frame, ensuring they align temporally with camera and IMU data.
beats.title: Sensor Timestamping and Frame Interpretation
beats.visualDirection: Display a timeline with synchronized sensor events, each marked with a timestamp and frame label, connected to a central synchronization node.

beats.claim: Reactive motion control adjusts robot behavior in real time based on immediate environmental feedback, enabling safe navigation in dynamic settings.
beats.example: A velocity controller reduces forward speed when a proximity sensor detects an obstacle within two meters, preventing collisions without full replanning.
beats.title: Reactive Motion Control Principles
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-view simulation of a robot approaching a wall, with a reactive control loop highlighted, displaying input sensor data, computed velocity, and output wheel commands.

beats.claim: Map building and localization enable robots to construct environmental models and determine their position within those models using sensor data.
beats.example: A SLAM algorithm fuses wheel odometry and camera images to update a grid map, then uses feature matching to locate the robot's current pose.
beats.title: Map Building and Localization
beats.visualDirection: Render a top-down map grid with a moving robot icon, showing how sensor observations incrementally fill in map cells and update the robot's position marker.

beats.claim: Path planning algorithms compute sequences of actions that guide robots from a start to a goal while avoiding obstacles and adapting to changes.
beats.example: A reactive planner recalculates a route when a moving pedestrian enters the robot's path, inserting a detour that maintains safety margins and task completion time.
beats.title: Path Planning in Dynamic Environments
beats.visualDirection: Display a navigation map with a planned path, a dynamic obstacle, and a revised path, using color coding to distinguish static obstacles, dynamic hazards, and planned trajectories.

beats.claim: Students implement various algorithms in simulation as well as on a real robot, allowing iterative testing before physical deployment.
beats.example: A navigation algorithm is first validated in a physics engine simulation, then deployed on a wheeled robot to verify real-world performance and adjust parameters accordingly.
beats.title: Simulation and Physical Deployment
beats.visualDirection: Show a split-screen comparison: left side shows a simulation environment with debug overlays, right side shows a physical robot with sensor data feeds and control interfaces.

beats.claim: Effective robot software development requires systematic evaluation of latency, dropped messages, sensor noise, actuator limits, safety boundaries, and simulation-to-physical gaps.
beats.example: A developer checks that message latency stays below 50 milliseconds, verifies sensor noise does not exceed calibration thresholds, and confirms safety zones are enforced before field testing.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Present a checklist graphic with five categories (latency, message integrity, sensor noise, actuator limits, safety boundaries), each with a pass/fail indicator and a brief validation method.

Explain how ROS 2 message contracts, coordinate transforms, and timestamped observations enable reliable robot software communication.
Apply reactive motion control and path planning concepts to simulate and evaluate robot navigation in dynamic environments.
